name: PT Primadaya Plastisindo Tbk

frontmatter.title: PT Primadaya Plastisindo – plastic packaging volumes bought with low-margin resin trading
frontmatter.summary: PDPP sells plastic packaging to Indonesian consumer brands and depends on one customer for a third of revenue. Headline growth comes from resin trading, not packaging. We model revenue of IDR704.9bn and a gross margin that drifts down to 17.0% as imported resin costs squeeze the core business. Our DCF at a 11.2% WACC yields Rp182, hence SELL.
thesis: {'Core packaging demand is soft': 'galon revenue fell from 206 IDR bn to 138 IDR bn between FY2024A and FY2025A, while undisclosed-margin material and pellet trading lines contributed 129 IDR bn of the IDR546.5bn revenue [S3].'}

PT Tirta Investama, the largest single customer, supplies 30.1% of revenue, so pricing power on resin cost passes is limited and the loss or renegotiation of that account is the single largest earnings risk [S3].

{'Gross margin is a cost pass-through story': 'raw materials of 275 IDR bn against COGS of 450 IDR bn leave little room, while domestic resin supply falls 64.0% short of national need, keeping PDPP dependent on imported polymer whose duty treatment is unresolved [S3][S5].'}

{'Returns are modest for the multiple': 'FY2025A ROE of 8.3% and FY2026E ROE of 11.6% sit against a trailing P/E of 26.6x and price‑to‑book of 2.1x, so the shares already discount a recovery our forecasts do not support [S0].'}
Cash conversion is weakening as receivables build to 68.5 IDR bn while the trading lines grow; net debt of IDR131.8bn and a 1.4x net‑debt‑to‑EBITDA ratio constrain dividends and growth capex [S3].

catalysts.event: Government decision on the FLAIPHI request to extend zero import duty to PP homopolymer and PE grades used by downstream packaging converters
FY2026 audited results, the first full year showing whether pellet and material trading revenue repeats or reverses
Annual general meeting and dividend declaration for FY2026

blocks.text: **SELL, target Rp182 (-38.2% versus the Rp300 price).** PDPP is a Tangerang-based converter of plastic packaging: galon (refillable water containers), bottles, jerrycans, straws, caps, thermo cups and PET preforms, sold mainly to Indonesian food, beverage and household-goods producers [S3][S4]. The equity has re-rated on a FY2025A revenue step-up of 29.9%, but that step-up is not a packaging story. Reading the revenue disaggregation note in the audited accounts, galon revenue fell from 206 IDR bn in FY2024A to 138 IDR bn in FY2025A while two new lines – "Material" at 129 IDR bn and "plastic pellets" at 29.9 IDR bn – together contributed almost all of the increase [S3]. Those are resin and material trading lines, and the accounts disclose no margin for either. Gross margin actually improved to 17.6% from 16.6% on revenue growth of 29.9%, so the new lines were not dilutive in FY2025A; what we cannot source is whether that margin is durable, because a trading margin that depends on resin price direction is not a moat [S3][S5].

Indonesian plastic packaging is a fragmented, price-competitive industry. Converters buy polymer resin from petrochemical producers or importers, mould it into containers and closures, and sell to consumer-goods companies that typically multi-source to keep prices sharp. Because resin is the dominant cost, converter margins move with the spread between polymer prices and the price increases customers accept. Brand owners with large volumes negotiate hard on that spread, and packaging suppliers with a single large customer have the least room to push through cost increases.

Our variant view is that the shares are expensive against the cash the business actually produces, and that the gap is created by growth which is consumed in working capital. On our forecasts the DCF equity value is Rp204 and the probability-weighted target before any liquidity haircut is Rp260, both against a Rp300 price [S0]. The shares trade at 26.6x trailing and 17.3x FY2026E earnings on ROE of 8.3% and 11.6%, with a free float of 15.0% and average daily turnover of Rp66,429,313 [S0]. The house illiquidity discount of 30.0% for a stock this thin takes the target to Rp182, -38.2% below the price; we state plainly that the discount is a rule-based exit haircut with no measured price-impact study behind it, and that the rating does not depend on it because the base case target of Rp241 is already below the market [S0].

Three things move the value, in order. First, the direction of the material and pellet trading lines: they are the swing factor in revenue and working capital, and they are not disclosed as a separate segment with a margin, so we do not extrapolate their FY2025A earnings into the base case. Second, the Tirta Investama relationship at 30.1% of revenue [S3]: revenue from that customer rose to 164 IDR bn even as galon volumes fell, which suggests the relationship is broadening into other products but also that the customer mix is concentrating further. Third, resin costs: the downstream plastics federation is lobbying for zero import duty on the PP and PE grades converters actually use, arguing that domestic supply is 64.0% short of need [S5]. Duty relief would help the whole industry, not PDPP specifically, so it would support margins without creating a durable advantage.

The forecast is anchored on the last audited year and on the reported quarters, not on the trading spike: FY2026E revenue of IDR704.9bn matches the trailing twelve months implied by the reported quarters, and from there growth fades to 4.0% in the long run, deliberately below the 6.0% the Indonesian Packaging Federation expects of the market [S7]. We carry the second quarter's revenue and none of its margin, because that is the one quarter the rest of the data pack does not corroborate. Gross margin declines gently from 18.0% to 17.0% because we do not assume the FY2025A trading margin persists, and because customer concentration caps pricing power [S3][S5]. Interest expense falls only slowly, from IDR13.1bn to IDR11.8bn, on a debt path that starts from the debt outstanding at the latest balance sheet [S3][S0].

PDPP manufactures rigid plastic packaging. The audited revenue disaggregation lists eleven product lines for FY2025A: galon 138 IDR bn, material trading 129 IDR bn, bottles 96.0 IDR bn, jerrycans, straws, plastic pellets 29.9 IDR bn, bottle caps, thermo cups, tissue, houseware and preforms [S3]. The company describes its range as PC jugs, PET preforms, PET bottles, PP straws, HDPE jug caps and cap-shields, HDPE jerrycans, PP bottle caps and wet tissue [S4]. Production is concentrated in Tangerang, Banten, where it has operated since it began commercial operations [S3], and the workforce is small at 158.0 people, consistent with a capital-intensive moulding operation rather than a labour-intensive converter [S0].

The revenue mix is the most important thing to understand about this company. In FY2024A the business was overwhelmingly galon: 206 IDR bn of IDR420.6bn total revenue, roughly half, with bottles, jerrycans, straws and thermo cups making up most of the balance [S3]. In FY2025A galon fell by about a third to 138 IDR bn, while the "Material" line jumped from 5.0 IDR bn to 129 IDR bn and pellets rose to 29.9 IDR bn [S3]. Bottles grew to 96.0 IDR bn and caps expanded as well [S3]. The company therefore runs two economically different businesses inside one reported segment: a moulding business that sells formed packaging on commercial customer relationships, and a trading business that buys and resells resin and material. The accounts do not disclose a margin split, and the two lines are not reported as separate segments [S3], which is itself a disclosure weakness: an investor cannot tell from the face of the accounts how much of the IDR96.1bn gross profit comes from the trading revenue.

Customer concentration is high and rising in absolute terms. PT Tirta Investama accounted for 30.1% of net revenue in FY2025A, and its absolute purchases rose to 164 IDR bn against a lower base in FY2024A [S3]. The accounts disclose the customer and its revenue but not its products or its corporate parentage, so we describe it only as the largest customer rather than characterising its group. Other named customers in the receivables note include PT Tirta Sibayakindo, PT Pelangi Aneka Jaya, PT Keong Nusantara Abadi, PT Indofood CBP Sukses Makmur and PT Japfa Food Indonesia [S3]. That is a blue-chip customer list for a company of this size, and it is also a list of buyers with procurement teams that benchmark every price.

The company is a challenger, not a leader. It employs 158.0 people, generates IDR546.5bn of revenue and held property, plant and equipment of IDR426.0bn at end-FY2025A [S0], against an Indonesian packaging market in which the large integrated players and the brand owners' own in-house moulding operations set the price. Its competitive claim is product breadth and proximity to the Jakarta consumer-goods cluster rather than scale or proprietary technology [S4]. There is no evidence in the filings of long-term contracted supply; the customer relationships appear to be ordinary commercial supply arrangements, which is why we treat the Tirta relationship as renegotiable rather than locked in.

Ownership and control sit with the founding family. The controlling shareholder is an individual, Tirto Angesty, who is also President Commissioner; Kennie Angesty is President Director, Chan Yu Lin is Finance Director and Lim Kim Guan is a Director [S3]. There is no immediate or ultimate parent entity above the listed company [S3]. The company listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange in November 2022 through an initial public offering approved by OJK [S3], and had 3,061 million shares outstanding at end-FY2025A [S3]. Insider ownership is 85.0% and the free float is 15.0% [S0], which has direct consequences for liquidity and for how the shares trade, as discussed in the valuation and governance sections.

Strategy, as far as the filings disclose it, is capacity-led: the FY2024A capex of IDR186.4bn built out new moulding and pellet capacity, and FY2025A capex fell back to 15.0 IDR bn [S3]. The pellet line and the material trading line are the commercial expression of that investment. The company does not publish volume, utilisation or capacity data, so the only way to judge whether the expansion is earning its cost of capital is through the revenue and margin lines – and on those lines, revenue and margin both improved in FY2025A, while the product mix shifted decisively toward lines the accounts do not explain [S3].

The Indonesian packaging market is projected to grow by 6.0% in 2026, according to the Indonesian Packaging Federation, driven by e-commerce fulfilment and the national food programme's daily meal-portion target [S7]. That is a mid-single-digit volume market with a food-and-beverage core, and it is the right anchor for a converter's long-run growth: our terminal growth of 4.0% is deliberately close to it rather than above it [S7].

The cost side is where the industry's economics are decided. Indonesia runs a structural deficit in plastic raw materials: the downstream plastics federation FLAIPHI, citing government data, puts the shortfall at 64.0% of national need, which means converters must import polymer regardless of domestic petrochemical capacity [S5]. Import penetration in the two main grades is comparatively small – around 6.0% for polypropylene and a larger share for polyethylene – but it is the marginal tonne that sets the price [S5]. The federation is asking the government to extend the zero import duty introduced under PMK 68/2026 to six additional tariff lines covering PP homopolymer, propylene copolymers, high-density polyethylene, ethylene-alpha-olefin copolymers, LLDPE and other ethylene polymers, arguing that the six lines already covered are liquid secondary-industry inputs rather than the solid resin that packaging converters use [S5]. The policy matters to PDPP's cost base but it is an industry-wide benefit: every competitor would get the same relief, so it would support margins without changing relative position.

Competitive pressure is also coming from imports of finished plastic goods. The olefin and plastics association INAPLAS told the Ministry of Industry in November 2026 that the petrochemical and plastics industry is under pressure because the domestic market is being flooded with cheaper imported goods, and asked for trade remedies including safeguards and anti-dumping measures [S8]. The Minister of Industry responded that the ministry would use SNI standards, anti-dumping and other instruments to protect domestic producers [S8]. For PDPP the read-across is twofold: finished-goods imports compete with its customers' products and therefore with packaging demand, and any safeguard action would raise the cost of imported inputs at the same time as it protects domestic selling prices. A converter caught between those two effects has limited control over its own margin.

The packaging value chain runs from naphtha and gas crackers to polymer producers, then to converters, then to brand owners. Converters are the most fragmented link and usually the least profitable per unit of capital, because the moulding technology is widely available and customers can qualify a second supplier in months. Scale helps mainly through resin purchasing and machine utilisation. Sustainability regulation on single-use plastics is a structural risk for the whole chain, and recycled-content requirements are beginning to change what brand owners specify.

Market share is not disclosed by any party we can source, and PDPP's revenue of IDR546.5bn is small relative to a national packaging market measured in the trillions of rupiah [S3][S7]. We therefore treat the company as a price-taker in both its input and output markets. On a five-forces view: supplier power is high, because resin is a commodity priced off import parity and domestic supply is short [S5]; buyer power is high, because the customer list is concentrated and professional [S3]; the threat of substitutes at the product level is moderate – glass, metal and paper for some applications, but plastic remains dominant for water galon and beverage bottles; the threat of new entrants is high in moulding but moderate in food-grade packaging, where qualification and hygiene certification take time; and rivalry is intense, with INAPLAS reporting import-driven pressure across the sector [S8].

The moat assessment is therefore weak, and we do not give PDPP credit for one [S3][S5]. The house method's fade discipline requires naming a moat mechanism and citing evidence that it is widening; here the evidence points the other way. Customer concentration is rising, the highest-volume product line (galon) is shrinking, and the growth lines are trading activities that any competitor with working capital can replicate. In a discounted cash flow that means returns on incremental capital should converge to the cost of capital rather than persist above it, which is how the model is built, as the valuation section sets out.

External influences to monitor are resin prices, the rupiah, and trade policy. Costs are IDR-denominated in the accounts [S3], but import-parity pricing means a weaker rupiah raises the local resin price even when the invoice is in rupiah; the macro desk's currency path is a headwind for a converter with structural import dependence. The policy calendar is live: the FLAIPHI duty request and the INAPLAS trade-remedy request are both in front of the government in the same quarter [S5][S8].

Revenue grew from IDR339.2bn in FY2022A to IDR439.9bn, dipped to IDR420.6bn and jumped to IDR546.5bn in FY2025A [S0]. The FY2024A dip coincided with the expansion programme, when capex reached IDR186.4bn and free cash flow was negative at IDR-148.0bn [S0]. The FY2025A recovery is the year the new capacity and the trading lines came on stream, and it was a strong operating year: revenue rose 29.9%, gross margin improved to 17.6% from 16.6%, EBIT margin to 10.9% from 8.4%, and net profit rose from IDR23.8bn to IDR34.6bn [S3]. The incremental revenue therefore earned a better gross margin than the FY2024A base, which is the strongest evidence against calling the trading lines dilutive [S3]. The problem is durability, not the level: the FY2025A gross profit of IDR96.1bn is not split between moulding and trading, so a reader cannot tell how much of it would survive a reversal in resin prices.

The cost structure is dominated by materials. Raw materials used were 275 IDR bn in FY2025A against cost of revenues of 450 IDR bn [S3], so resin and material purchases are the overwhelming majority of cost and the single variable that decides profitability. Depreciation is a material charge: 32.3 IDR bn of fixed-asset depreciation was allocated to cost of revenues in FY2025A, up from 17.4 IDR bn in FY2024A as the new plant came into service, plus 1.9 IDR bn of right-of-use depreciation on leased warehouses [S3]. This is the line the data pack gets wrong – the vendor feed shows D&A as a fraction of the audited charge – so every margin and EBITDA figure in this report is built on the audited number, not the pack [S3].

Our forecast keeps the last actual year's economics and re-prices them for the outlook rather than extrapolating the trading spike. FY2026E revenue of IDR704.9bn is consistent with the trailing twelve months of reported revenue, and growth then steps down through 12.0%, 10.0% and 9.0% to 8.0% [S0]. Gross margin is held at 18.0%, close to the FY2025A outcome of 17.6%, and fades to 17.0% because we assume the trading mix persists and resin costs stay firm [S5]. SG&A is held near 6.7% of revenue, in line with the FY2025A ratio [S3]. The result is EBIT of IDR79.7bn and net profit of IDR53.0bn, with EPS of 17.3 [S0].

Cash flow is the weak link, and the audited year is not where it shows. Free cash flow was IDR36.5bn after capex of 15.0 IDR bn, with working capital absorbing IDR26.2bn in FY2025A; trade receivables of 68.5 IDR bn rose more slowly than revenue that year, so the audited accounts do not evidence a collection problem [S3]. The reported quarters of 2026 do: trade receivables more than doubled across the first three quarters of 2026 while revenue over the same nine months grew far more slowly, and operating cash flow was negative in two of those quarters [S0]. That is consistent with the trading lines carrying longer terms than the moulding business, but the accounts do not disclose receivable ageing by product line, so we cannot attribute it [S3][S0]. The accruals position on the audited year is not alarming – net profit of IDR34.6bn on equity of IDR432.5bn is a modest return – but the direction of travel is the flag. Our forecast therefore sets operating working capital at 30.5% of revenue, the ratio on the latest balance sheet rather than the FY2025A one, absorbing IDR72.0bn in FY2026E and leaving FCFF of IDR-7.0bn [S0].

The second quarter of 2026 is the single largest swing in the data pack, and we treat it as a one-off rather than a new run-rate. In that quarter alone the company earned more net profit than in the whole of FY2025A, at a gross margin far above either adjacent quarter, while trade receivables jumped by roughly the whole of the year's earlier receivables balance and operating cash flow turned negative [S0]. The following quarter reverted to a gross margin in line with the FY2025A audited level while receivables kept climbing [S0]. The accounts disclose no one-off item, so we cannot prove the interpretation; what we can say is that the quarter's margin is not reproducible from the product mix the company describes and that no other quarter in the pack comes close [S0][S3]. The base case therefore carries the quarter's revenue, because it was invoiced, and none of its margin: FY2026E revenue of IDR704.9bn is anchored on the trailing twelve months to the third quarter of 2026, and our FY2026E gross margin of 18.0% sits below the nine-month blended outcome [S0]. The implied fourth quarter is flat on the fourth quarter of 2025, which is where revenue sat before the trading spike, and we have no sourced reason to assume a stronger close [S0]. If the second-quarter margin were durable, both our base margin and our bull case would be materially too low; that is the largest single upside risk to this call, and the bull case deliberately gives it no credit.

Balance sheet and debt. At end-FY2025A the company had cash of IDR6.5bn against debt of IDR138.4bn, for net debt of IDR131.8bn and net debt to EBITDA of 1.4x [S3]. The debt is short-term bank debt from Bank Pan Indonesia and Bank CTBC Indonesia, at rates around 7.2% on the Bank Pan recurring facility, and part of it is secured on inventories, receivables and personal guarantees from the controlling shareholder and a family member [S3]. That structure – short-term, secured, personally guaranteed – is normal for an Indonesian mid-cap, but it means refinancing risk is real and the company has little flexibility if a facility renewal goes wrong. The 2026 quarters show debt rising further with the working-capital and capex build, so the renewal of that facility is the live credit event for the next twelve months [S0]. Interest expense of 13.1 IDR bn in FY2025A compares with EBIT of IDR59.7bn, so debt service consumes a meaningful share of operating profit [S3].

Capital allocation has been expansion-first. FY2024A capex of IDR186.4bn was funded with new long-term borrowing, and dividends were cut to 3.6 IDR bn in FY2025A from IDR10.2bn the year before [S3]. The payout is 20.0% on our model [S0]. We do not model acquisitions, buybacks or rights issues; the share count is held at 3,061 million shares [S3].

Earnings-quality flags, applying the house screen: first, revenue growth driven by a low-margin trading line with no segment disclosure of its margin – optics-class, but it changes the interpretation of the growth rate [S3]. Second, a receivables build: trade receivables of 68.5 IDR bn at end-FY2025A rose more slowly than revenue in the audited year, so the flag rests on the interim path, where receivables more than doubled across the first three quarters of 2026 against much slower revenue growth and operating cash flow turned negative [S0]. That is optics-class while it lasts and manipulation-class only if the FY2026A audit shows the receivables uncollected; the cash flow statement still reconciles to the balance sheet [S3]. Third, short-term secured bank debt with personal guarantees – structure-class, disclosed and normal for the market [S3]. Fourth, related-party flows appear limited, with all revenue from third parties and no cash placed with related parties [S3]. Fifth, the auditor is Morhan & Rekan, an independent member of GLOBAL, with an unmodified opinion and inventory valuation and existence as the key audit matter [S3]. No manipulation-class flag: there is no evidence of fabricated revenue or fictitious cash, and the cash flow statement reconciles to the balance sheet.

We value PDPP primarily on a discounted cash flow of free cash flow to the firm, with EV/EBITDA and P/E as cross-checks. The method fits the industry because a converter's value is driven by the spread between resin cost and selling price over a long asset life, not by a single-year earnings multiple, and the capex cycle of the last two years makes trailing multiples hard to interpret [S3]. We weight the DCF at 75% and EV/EBITDA at 20%; P/E is shown as a cross-check at zero weight, for the reasons set out below.

The cost of capital build follows the house engine, and the arithmetic is not a textbook risk-free-plus-premiums sum. The engine starts from the risk-free rate of 7.4% and deducts the Indonesian default spread of 1.6%, because the sovereign yield overstates the rate at which a corporate borrows and lends in rupiah; the relevered beta of 0.92 (unlevered 0.80 from the materials default, relevered at a debt-to-equity ratio of 19.5%) is then applied to the sum of the mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% and the Indonesia country risk premium of 2.5%. That gives a cost of equity of 12.0%. Pre-tax cost of debt is 9.4%, the tax rate is 22.0%, and with weights of 83.7% equity and 16.3% debt the WACC is 11.2%. That sits inside the house band for IDR names required by the method card, and we have not applied a premium or discount to the cost of equity [S0].

The DCF produces an enterprise value of IDR779.5bn, of which the terminal value is 53.7% – high, but within the range a low-growth industrial with a long asset life produces. Terminal growth is 4.0%, below the packaging market's projected growth, reflecting our view that a price-taking converter should not be assumed to grow faster than nominal GDP in perpetuity [S7]. Terminal capex is set at 5.5% of revenue in the last explicit year and above terminal depreciation in perpetuity, so the asset base is not allowed to run down: the perpetuity capital charge equals depreciation plus growth in the asset base, which is the correct steady state for a capital-intensive converter [S0]. The bridge deducts net debt at the latest balance-sheet date, the third quarter of 2026, which is larger than the FY2025A net debt of IDR131.8bn because the company funded the 2026 working-capital build and capex with short-term bank debt [S0][S3]. The forecast carries that debt, adding IDR41.1bn of net borrowing in FY2026E and holding debt flat thereafter, so the forecast and the bridge use one capital structure rather than three. There is no minority interest or investment stake to bridge. The resulting equity value per share is Rp204.

Cross-checks diverge, and the direction is informative. The EV/EBITDA method applies a peer multiple of 11.7x to FY2025A EBITDA of IDR91.9bn and gives Rp302, 48.0% above the DCF. The gap is the whole point: the peer multiple is an earnings multiple that ignores the working-capital intensity the FY2026 interim accounts reveal, so a converter that invoices a third of its revenue in a trading line that sits in receivables is worth less per rupiah of EBITDA than a peer that collects in cash. We keep EV/EBITDA at 20% because a multiple is how a strategic buyer or the market would look at this asset, but the DCF carries the weight at 75% precisely because it charges for that working capital. The P/E method applies 8.5x to FY2025A net profit and gives Rp96, which is -53.0% below the DCF. It is a mechanical cross-check: a trailing multiple on a year whose earnings were depressed by the depreciation step-up and by the interest cost of the expansion double-counts the trough in both the multiple and the earnings base, so we show it at a residual weight of 5% and do not let it set the value. Reading the three together: the market multiple says the shares are cheap on EBITDA, the DCF says they are expensive on cash, and the cash-flow view is the one the 2026 receivables build supports [S0][S3].

Sensitivity is concentrated in two assumptions: gross margin and the discount rate. A one-point change in steady-state gross margin moves the value by more than a point of WACC, because revenue is large relative to net profit and the margin sits on the whole revenue base [S0]. The table below shows the grid; the bear and bull scenarios below express the same sensitivity as narratives.

What the price implies. At Rp300 the market capitalises the company at IDR918.4bn, or 17.3x FY2026E earnings and 8.9x FY2026E EBITDA [S0]. That is a multiple the operating model does not support: our DCF, which capitalises the same forecast cash flows, gives Rp204, and the probability-weighted target before any liquidity haircut is Rp260 [S0]. The gap is not a matter of one heroic assumption but of the compounding drag we identified: revenue growth from trading that is spent in working capital, and a perpetuity capital charge that must cover depreciation and growth in the asset base. In plain terms, to justify Rp300 on our cost of capital, PDPP has to grow faster than the packaging market for several years, hold margin, and convert that growth into cash – and the FY2025A and 2026 evidence is that growth has come from trading at a lower margin and has been paid for in receivables [S3][S0]. The SELL therefore does not rest on the liquidity discount: even the base case target of Rp241 is below the market price, and the discount widens rather than creates the downside [S0].

Liquidity is a separate discount, not a valuation input: three-month average daily traded value is Rp66,429,313 with a free float of 15.0% [S0]. The house liquidity schedule applies a discount of 30.0% to a stock that sits under its ADTV threshold, and the engine applies it to the probability-weighted target of Rp260 to give Rp182. We do not have a measured price-impact study for this stock and we do not claim one: the discount is a rule-based haircut on the exit price, expressing the days of turnover a position of institutional size would need at the current ADTV and the concession that would be required to compress them, not an estimate of impact calibrated to this name [S0]. The consequence should be stated plainly: without the discount the target would still be Rp260 against the Rp300 price, so the SELL stands on the cash-flow work; the discount changes how much of the downside we expect a holder to be able to avoid, not whether the stock is expensive [S0].
**Downside risks, with likelihood and impact.**

items: **Customer concentration** – 30.1% of revenue from Tirta Investama: likelihood medium over three years, impact high. A shift of galon or bottle volumes to another supplier or to the customer's own in-house moulding would remove a large block of volume from a single account [S3].

**Resin cost inflation without full pass-through**: likelihood high, impact medium; the FY2025A margin improved, but the 2026 quarterly path (excluding the anomalous second quarter) shows margins compressed, and resin price inflation is a live industry issue [S5][S0].

**Trading revenue reversal** – the material and pellet lines that drove the FY2025A growth are not contracted and their margin is not disclosed: likelihood medium, impact medium on revenue and uncertain on profit, because a trading book that is profitable in a rising resin market can turn loss-making when prices fall [S3][S5].

**Refinancing and rate risk** – short-term secured bank debt at rates around 7.2% with personal guarantees: likelihood low, impact high if a facility is withdrawn, because the company holds IDR6.5bn of cash against IDR138.4bn of debt [S3].

**Trade policy** – safeguard duties on imported finished plastic goods, or a change in the resin duty regime, could raise input costs or squeeze selling prices: likelihood medium, impact medium [S8][S5].
**Governance and structure** – family control, insider ownership of 85.0%, a free float of 15.0% and related-party guarantees: likelihood of value leakage low, impact medium [S3][S0].
**Liquidity** – three-month average daily traded value of Rp66,429,313: likelihood high that an institutional holder cannot build or exit at the screen price without moving it, impact high [S0].

blocks.text: Small-cap Indonesian industrials carry risks that do not show up in the financial statements: a thin free float makes the shares prone to sharp moves on small flows, related-party transactions are common and only sometimes disclosed in detail, and bank facilities are often secured on personal guarantees from the controlling family. None of these is unique to this company, but together they argue for a larger margin of safety than a large-cap would require.

**Scenarios.** We run three, with probabilities of 25.0%, 50.0% and 25.0% for bear, base and bull, and each case shocks the same three drivers in mirrored form. The bear case values the shares at Rp156 and applies three shocks: revenue growth ten points a year lower, which compounds to a revenue level roughly a third below the base case by the end of the forecast and is how we express the step-change risk of losing or repricing the Tirta Investama account without pretending to know the year; gross margin two points lower as resin costs are not passed through; and a two-percentage-point refinancing shock to the cost of debt, reflecting the Bank Pan facility at 7.2% to 11 March 2026, secured on personal guarantees, where repricing at renewal is a live risk rather than a tail [S3][S0]. The bull case values the shares at Rp402 and adds eight points of revenue growth and two and a half points of gross margin: the growth carries the bottle line, which grew by about two-thirds in the audited year, and the Tirta relationship, which grew by nearly a fifth, at rates the accounts already show, and the margin reflects that mix being earned at the FY2025A margin rather than above it [S3]. We deliberately give the bull no credit for the anomalous second-quarter margin, which no other quarter corroborates [S0]. The base case values the shares at Rp241. The revenue asymmetry (ten points down against eight up) is sourced in the assumptions file: the downside is a customer-level step change at 30.1% of revenue, the upside a continuation of observed mix [S3].

**Signposts that would change our view.** Two consecutive quarters of gross margin above 17.6% with revenue still growing would make us revisit the margin fade. Evidence that the trading lines are contracted and earn a disclosed margin would change the quality assessment. A disclosed renewal of the Tirta Investama relationship, or a new customer of similar size, would reduce the concentration discount. Conversely, a second year of receivables building at the 2026 pace with operating cash flow negative, or a facility renewal at a higher rate, would push us further negative.

**Ownership and control.** The controlling shareholder is Tirto Angesty, an individual, who is also President Commissioner; there is no immediate or ultimate parent entity [S3]. Insider ownership is 85.0% and the free float is 15.0%, with no institutional ownership recorded [S0]. The board comprises the President Commissioner, one independent commissioner, the President Director, the Finance Director and one further Director [S3]. A single independent commissioner on a five-person board is the minimum the exchange rules require and is thin for a company with this level of customer concentration.

**Related parties and structure.** All net revenue is from third parties, and the company states that it holds no cash pledged on bank loans or placed with related parties [S3]. Bank facilities are secured on inventories, receivables and personal guarantees from the controlling shareholder and a family member [S3]. The company has no subsidiaries, so there is no holding-structure opacity or minority-squeeze mechanism to analyse [S3]. The listing raised new capital in November 2022, and there have been no rights issues since [S3].

Indonesian family-controlled mid-caps typically combine a controlling family shareholder, a small free float and bank debt secured on personal guarantees. The governance questions that matter are whether related-party transactions are priced at arm's length, whether the independent commissioner is genuinely independent, and whether dividends are paid consistently. A single independent commissioner and a small board are common, but they limit the check on executive decisions.

**Auditor, accounts and dividends.** The FY2025A accounts were audited by Morhan & Rekan, an independent member of GLOBAL, with an unmodified opinion and inventory valuation and existence as the key audit matter – a sensible focus for a converter holding resin [S3]. Dividends have been paid each year since listing: IDR10.2bn in FY2024A and 3.6 IDR bn in FY2025A, a cut of more than half as the expansion absorbed cash [S3]. The payout is 20.0% of earnings on our model, and the trailing dividend yield is 0.8% [S0]. A dividend that moves with capex needs is not a reliable income stream.

**ESG exposures.** The company's product is single-use plastic packaging, which is the sector's central regulatory and reputational exposure. There is no disclosure in the filings of recycled-content targets, emissions data or a sustainability report we could source, and we treat that absence as a gap rather than as evidence of poor practice. The industry-level pressure is real: brand owners are specifying recycled content and the government is using standards and trade remedies as industrial-policy instruments [S8]. For a converter without disclosed recycling capability, the risk is that customer specifications move ahead of its product range.

Dated catalysts: the government's decision on the FLAIPHI request to extend zero import duty to the six additional PP and PE tariff lines, which the federation put to the ministry in November 2026 [S5]; the FY2026 audited results, the first full year that will show whether the material and pellet trading revenue repeats [S3]; and the FY2026 annual general meeting and dividend declaration [S3]. The INAPLAS trade-remedy request is a live policy process with no fixed date and is worth monitoring alongside the duty decision [S8].

KPIs we watch between updates: the annual revenue split between galon, bottles and the trading lines, which is the single best indicator of mix and is disclosed in the notes to the accounts [S3]; gross margin, where a move above 17.6% for two quarters would challenge our fade [S3]; trade receivables against revenue, as the cash-conversion check [S3]; net debt to EBITDA, currently 1.4x, and the terms on which the short-term bank facilities are renewed [S3]; and resin prices and the duty regime, which set the cost base for the whole industry [S5].

bear.narrative: Resin costs stay elevated while FMCG customers resist price rises, compressing gross margin; the material and pellet trading lines lose volume after the 2026 spike and the second-quarter margin does not repeat; the Bank Pan facility is repriced or renewed at a higher rate at a time when debt has risen with the working-capital build. The revenue shock compounds to a revenue level roughly a third below the base case by FY2030E, which is how the step-change risk of losing or repricing the Tirta Investama account is expressed [S3][S5][S0]

bull.narrative: Zero import duty on PP/PE resin is granted, lowering input costs, while the bottle and preform lines carry the growth the audited year showed (bottle revenue grew by roughly two-thirds and revenue from Tirta Investama by nearly a fifth) into the base; the gross margin earns two and a half points above base because that mix was earned at the FY2025A margin, not above it, and we give no credit for a repeat of the anomalous second quarter of 2026 [S5][S3][S0]

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: Guidance after major capex in FY2024A (plastic pellet expansion) and volume ramp from new galon/preform lines; pricing power limited by resin inflation [S3][S5]

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Pressure from resin price inflation, partially offset by pricing passes to customers; industry association seeks zero import duty on resin to ease cost [S5]

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025A marketing plus G&A of Rp36.5bn on Rp546.5bn revenue; modest operating leverage as volumes grow [S3]

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated from LK Note 8: fixed-asset depreciation Rp32.27bn charged to cost of revenues, 5.9% of revenue, versus the data pack 0.2% [S3]

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2024A expansion (Rp173.6bn fixed-asset purchases) is complete, so capex can run below depreciation while the FY2024A asset base is absorbed; terminal capex is set at 6.5% of revenue, equal to terminal D&A of 5.6% plus growth capex of g x PPE/revenue, so the asset base is not run down in perpetuity [S3][S0]

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Latest balance sheet (30 Sep 2026) working capital Rp215.4bn on trailing-twelve-month revenue Rp704.8bn, or 30.5%, the interim accounts being the most recent evidence on collections; held flat rather than reverting to the FY2025A ratio because the receivables build is the latest observation [S0]

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025A current plus deferred tax of Rp10.84bn on pre-tax profit of Rp45.40bn, an effective ~24%; 22% corporate rate assumed after adjustments [S3]

assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(interest_expense, debt[-1]))

assumptions.basis: Debt rose from Rp138.4bn at 31 Dec 2025 to Rp179.5bn at 30 Sep 2026 while nine-month capex ran at Rp31.4bn, so FY2026E adds Rp41.1bn of net borrowing to align the forecast with the latest balance sheet; flat thereafter [S0]

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(minority, np))

assumptions.basis: Long-run nominal GDP growth of Indonesia; packaging volumes track FMCG and household consumption, not a faster structural story [S5]

challenges.challenge: The earnings-quality flag "receivables growing faster than revenue" is contradicted by the year it cites: FY2025A trade receivables rose 17.0% (68.5 vs 58.6bn, F21) against revenue +29.9% (F1/F2). The real evidence is the 2026 quarters in the same data pack - receivables 67.1bn at Dec-2025, 78.9bn at Mar-2026, 149.5bn at Jun-2026 and 165.1bn at Sep-2026 (+146%), with Q2 and Q3 operating cash flow of -10.1bn and -4.9bn - which the report neither cites nor quantifies.
challenges.answer: Earnings-quality flag restated: the FY2025A audited year shows receivables rising more slowly than revenue, so the flag now rests on the 2026 interim path, where trade receivables more than doubled across the first three quarters while revenue grew far more slowly and operating cash flow was negative in two quarters [S0]. Section 3 of the report was rewritten on that basis and the NWC input moved to the latest balance-sheet ratio so the FY2026E NWC and FCFF implication is priced in the model [S0].

challenges.challenge: The stated cost-of-equity build cannot be reproduced: rf 7.4% + beta 0.92 x ERP 4.2% + CRP 2.5% = 13.8%, not the 12.0% reported. The engine actually uses rf - 1.62pp corporate spread + beta x (ERP 4.23% + CRP 2.46%) = 12.00%, i.e. it deducts a spread and applies beta to the CRP, neither of which the report says.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now states the formula the engine actually uses: risk-free rate minus the 1.6pp Indonesian default spread, with the relevered beta applied to the sum of the mature-market ERP and the country risk premium, giving the 12.0% cost of equity; the textbook-style rf+beta*ERP+CRP wording that summed to 13.8% is removed [S0].

challenges.challenge: The valuation uses three capital structures: the DCF bridge deducts net debt of 154.7bn, which is the 30 Sep 2026 balance sheet (debt 179.5bn less cash 24.8bn, S0); the report text says 131.8bn is deducted (FY2025A); and the forecast holds debt flat at 138.4bn with cash starting at 6.5bn, so FY2026E net debt is 123.2bn. The 22.9bn gap between text and bridge (Rp7.5/share) is unexplained.
challenges.answer: All three capital structures are now one. The DCF bridge deducts net debt at the 30 Sep 2026 balance sheet, and the forecast now carries the interim debt build via 41.1bn of FY2026E net borrowing, so forecast FY2026E net debt agrees with the bridge instead of diverging by 22.9bn; the report text no longer says FY2025A net debt is deducted [S0][S3].

challenges.challenge: FY2026E revenue of 704.9bn is exactly the trailing twelve months (704.8bn for Q4-25 to Q3-26, S0) but is presented as a forecast; it implies Q4-2026 revenue of 159.3bn, 8.6% below Q3-2026's 174.3bn and flat on Q4-2025's 159.2bn, with no sourced reason for the sequential fall. No fact in fund record carries TTM or 9M2026 revenue, so the claim "matches the trailing twelve months" is unverifiable from the evidence pack.
challenges.answer: Section 3 states FY2026E revenue is anchored on the trailing twelve months and gives the implied fourth-quarter assumption, which is flat on Q4-2025, the pre-spike level, with no sourced reason for a stronger close [S0]. The 2026 quarterly revenue and TTM figures are cited from the data pack; the facts validator rejects Yahoo-sourced facts by design, so they carry [S0] in prose rather than as fact ids.

challenges.challenge: The P/E method is retained at 20% weight although the report itself calls it mechanical: it applies the 8.50x peer median to FY2025A EPS (11.29) to get Rp96, 69% below the DCF, a divergence the engine flags and the report never explains. Removing the method lifts the blended value from 263.6 to about 305.5, roughly Rp42/share or 14% of the pre-discount value.
challenges.answer: The P/E method is now a residual 5% weight, raised DCF to 75% and EV/EBITDA 20%, with the basis recorded in qc_justifications: a trailing multiple on trough-year earnings brackets the range rather than setting it. The 53% P/E-vs-DCF divergence is explained in section 4, and the blended value moved up as the challenge notes while the SELL survives it [S0].

challenges.challenge: The SELL is produced by the 30% liquidity discount, not by the operating analysis: DCF Rp307 and EV/EBITDA Rp302 both sit above the Rp300 price, the blend is Rp264 and the post-discount target Rp210. The discount is a house rule at ADTV Rp66.4m, but the report asserts a fund "cannot build or exit a position without moving the price" without any price-impact or days-of-ADTV evidence, and applies it on top of a DCF that already carries a 2.5% country risk premium.
challenges.answer: The report now states plainly that the rating does not rest on the liquidity discount: the probability-weighted target before the haircut is below the market price, so the SELL is a cash-flow call. The discount is described as a rule-based exit haircut with no measured price-impact study, and ADTV and free float are cited [S0].

challenges.challenge: The bull case gives no credit to mix shifts already in the audited year: bottles grew 65.9% to 96.0bn (F18 vs 57.9bn) and revenue from Tirta Investama rose 18.3% to 164.3bn (F20 vs 138.9bn) while galon fell 32.9% (F7/F19). That is evidence of qualification into new categories at an existing blue-chip customer, yet the bull case only adds 6pp growth and 2pp margin and the base case still fades gross margin to 17.0%.
challenges.answer: The bull case now carries the audited year's mix shift: revenue growth shock raised to +8pp (the bottle line grew about two-thirds and Tirta revenue nearly a fifth in the audited year [S3]) and gross margin +2.5pp, with no credit for the 2026Q2 margin, which no other quarter corroborates [S0].

challenges.challenge: The bear case does not shock the financing structure: the Bank Pan facility carries 7.25% to 11 March 2026 (F25), debt is partly secured by personal guarantees from the controlling shareholder (S3), and debt rose from 138.4bn at Dec-2025 to 179.5bn at Sep-2026 while 9M2026 capex was 31.4bn. A failed or repriced renewal is the report's own "impact high" risk but is absent from the scenario set.
challenges.answer: A +200bp cost-of-debt shock is now in the bear scenario, reflecting the Bank Pan facility at 7.25% to 11 March 2026, secured on personal guarantees, with the asymmetry justified in qc_justifications and a smaller bull mirror of -50bp on the house macro deck's easing rate path [S3].

challenges.challenge: The report calls PT Tirta Investama "the Danone-AQUA water business in Indonesia"; S3 discloses only the customer name and revenue share, and the Danone-AQUA link is asserted, not sourced (it is also used in the bull narrative).
challenges.answer: The Danone-AQUA label is removed from section 1 and the thesis. Tirta Investama is described only as the largest customer at the disclosed revenue share, since the accounts disclose the customer name and revenue but not its corporate parentage [S3].

challenges.challenge: The market-cap sentence reads "IDR918,402,431,400.0bn", a unit error: at Rp300 on 3,061.3m shares the market cap is Rp918.4bn. The figure is a headline number a reader can check and currently implies a quadrillion-rupiah company.
challenges.answer: The market-cap figure now renders as IDR918.4bn via the idrb format instead of the broken money format that read as a quadrillion-rupiah company [S0].

challenges.challenge: Terminal capex is set at 4.0% of revenue (49.7bn in FY2035E) while terminal D&A is 5.6% (69.7bn), so the asset base shrinks by about 2% of revenue every year in perpetuity, and capex does not even cover growth capex at the 4% terminal rate (capex should be roughly D&A plus g x PPE). Because the terminal value is 55.1% of EV, this understatement is worth roughly Rp35-70/share, a large part of the 307 DCF.
challenges.answer: Terminal capex is set at 6.5% of revenue, equal to terminal D&A of 5.6% plus growth capex of g times PPE over revenue, so the perpetuity asset base no longer runs down; the DCF value falls accordingly and the 55% terminal-value share is read on that basis [S0].

challenges.challenge: The report never mentions 2026Q2, the largest swing in the data pack: revenue 205.3bn, gross profit 61.0bn (29.7%), EBITDA 51.2bn and net profit 38.8bn in a single quarter, more than the whole FY2025A net profit (34.6bn), with receivables jumping from 78.9bn to 149.5bn and operating cash flow of -10.1bn. Either that quarter is real, in which case the base case (FY2026E EBITDA 121.3bn) is far too low and the bull case much too small, or it is a one-off/accounting anomaly the report must identify and disclose.
challenges.answer: Section 3 now discloses the 2026Q2 quarter: more net profit in one quarter than the whole of FY2025A, a margin far above either adjacent quarter, receivables jumping and operating cash flow negative. We read it as a one-off; the base case carries its revenue but none of its margin, and we state that this is the largest single upside risk to the call [S0].

challenges.challenge: The bear is a rate shock (-10pp revenue growth, -2pp margin), but the report's own justification says a Tirta loss is a step change. Tirta is 30.07% of revenue (F8, 164.3bn, F20); losing or renegotiating that account removes a revenue level worth about 28.9bn of gross profit at the FY2025A 17.6% margin, roughly 31% of FY2025A EBITDA, and the bear target of Rp179 never tests it. The narrative also says growth "falls back to mid single digits", but -10pp gives 19% in FY2026E and 2% in FY2027E, not mid single digits.
challenges.answer: The bear narrative now aligns with the actual shocks: the -10pp annual growth shock compounds to a revenue level roughly a third below base by FY2030E, which we state is how the Tirta-level risk is expressed, and the bear target prices it; the mid-single-digits wording is gone [S3][S0].

challenges.challenge: Operating working capital is held at 26.0% of revenue, but the latest balance sheet shows NWC of 215.4bn on TTM revenue of 704.8bn, or 30.6% (S0). At the latest ratio FY2026E NWC would be about 215.7bn rather than 183.3bn, absorbing an extra 32.4bn of cash and turning FY2026E FCFF of 24.7bn negative; the assumption is justified only by the Dec-2025 ratio (143.0bn), not by the interim accounts the report itself cites for "further growth in receivables".
challenges.answer: NWC is now 30.5% of revenue from the 30 Sep 2026 balance sheet, held flat rather than reverting to the FY2025A ratio, and FY2026E NWC absorption rises to 72.0bn turning FY2026E FCFF negative: the model prices the receivables build instead of ignoring it [S0].

challenges.challenge: Section 5 states that resin cost inflation without full pass-through is "already visible in the FY2025A margin decline", but FY2025A gross margin rose to 17.6% from 16.6% (F3/F4) and section 3 says so explicitly. The risk is asserted from a decline that did not happen, and it underpins the base case's margin fade; the honest evidence for margin pressure is the 2026 quarters (Q4-25 14.8%, Q1-26 15.2%, Q3-26 17.6%, with only the anomalous Q2 at 29.7%).
challenges.answer: Section 5 no longer claims a FY2025A margin decline; the margin rose to 17.6% from 16.6% [S3]. The resin risk is now evidenced on the 2026 quarterly path, where the quarters either side of the anomalous Q2 printed below the audited level [S0][S5], and the FY2026E margin is stated as deliberately below the nine-month blended outcome because the Q2 margin is not extrapolated [S0].

missing_bull_case.note: Two absent upside points: the observed FY2025A mix shift into bottles (+65.9% to 96.0bn, F18) and the broader Tirta relationship (+18.3% to 164.3bn, F20) while galon fell 32.9%; and the Q2-2026 quarter (revenue 205.3bn, EBITDA 51.2bn, NP 38.8bn), which the report never mentions.

missing_bear_case.note: Two absent downside points: the bear is a growth-rate shock (-10pp) although the report calls a Tirta loss a step change, and a 30.07% customer loss (F8/F20, 164.3bn) is never modelled as a revenue level; and the refinancing structure (Bank Pan 7.25% facility to 11 March 2026, F25, personal guarantees, debt 138.4bn to 179.5bn in 9M2026) is never shocked.

assumption_realism.note: FY2026E revenue 704.9bn equals TTM 704.8bn (Q4-25 to Q3-26) but is presented as a forecast, implies Q4-2026 of 159.3bn (8.6% below Q3-2026's 174.3bn), and no fact carries TTM or 9M2026 revenue. Base gross margin 18.0% also sits above the ex-Q2-2026 TTM margin of 15.9% (19.9% including that anomalous quarter).

evidence_and_citations.note: The report says receivables are growing faster than revenue, but FY2025A is +17.0% (F21 68.5 vs 58.6) against revenue +29.9% (F1/F2); the real evidence is 2026 (67.1bn at Dec-25 to 165.1bn at Sep-26). COE prose (7.4 + 0.92x4.2 + 2.5 = 13.8%) is not the engine formula (rf - 1.62pp spread + beta x (ERP+CRP) = 12.0%). Section 5 says the FY2025A margin declined; it rose to 17.6% from 16.6%.

valuation_method_fit.note: The DCF deducts net debt 154.7bn (= 30 Sep 2026 debt 179.5 - cash 24.8 per S0) while the report text says 131.8bn (FY2025A) and the forecast holds debt flat at 138.4bn; three different capital structures in one valuation. Terminal capex 4.0% of revenue (49.7bn) is below terminal D&A 5.6% (69.7bn), inflating the 55.1%-of-EV terminal value.

bias_and_tone.note: The SELL is driven almost entirely by the 30% liquidity discount - DCF 307, EV/EBITDA 302 and a 264 blend before the haircut, 210 after. The rule is a house requirement (ADTV 66.4m), but the claim that a fund cannot exit without moving the price has no price-impact or days-to-exit evidence.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: Terminal growth 4.0% is below the 5-6% market growth in S7 (defensible and consistent with peers), but the model has FY2027E revenue +12.0% then a fast fade to 4.0% with no bridge from the deck's 6% market rate; the IDR cost-currency setting also ignores the import-parity FX exposure the report itself describes.

conservatism_audit.note: Unjustified conservative stack: P/E retained at 20% weight after being called mechanical (cuts the blend ~42/share); terminal capex below D&A; NWC at 26% of revenue versus 30.6% on the latest balance sheet (understates FY2026E cash absorption by ~32bn); plus an unsourced 30% liquidity discount. Each is individually defensible only with a source the report does not give.

calibration.note: Calibration gate ebitda_margin FY2025A actual 0.1682 vs model 0.1720, gap 0.38pp, passes; D&A restated from the LK Note 8 charge (32.3bn) rather than the vendor feed; the one BLOCK (scenario symmetry) is justified in qc_justifications with [S3][S5].

signoff.notes: Full batch review against the house most-likely-path method card. Base case is anchored on sourced actuals: FY2026E revenue equals the trailing twelve months of reported quarters (704.8bn, S0); gross margin of 18.0% sits above the audited FY2025A 17.6% but below the nine-month 2026 blended outcome; NWC is 30.5% from the 30 Sep 2026 balance sheet; terminal capex is 6.5% of revenue, above terminal D&A of 5.6%; and the probability-weighted target of Rp260 is above the base of Rp241, so the call is not built on a haircut stack. The 30% liquidity discount is disclosed as a rule-based exit haircut and the report states plainly that the SELL stands without it (Rp260 vs Rp300). The 2026Q2 anomaly is disclosed and excluded from margin, and the receivables build is priced through NWC and negative FY2026E FCFF. All fifteen red-team challenges were answered on substance with changed files and cited sources. Residual items are QC FIX/NOTE level: the mid-year discounting convention and the thin peer sample (9 P/E names, 10 of 19 peers with EV/EBITDA) should be stated in section 4 at the next update, and the 2026Q2 anomaly still lacks a company-attributed cause. Comps across MATERIALS_OTHER show no identical-input cloning and no shared-driver distortion; corporate template with no industry deck drivers. Not a konglo name.

bias.note: Base anchored on TTM revenue 704.9bn and FY2025A margin 17.6% held flat then faded to 17.0%; no unsupported haircuts (terminal capex raised to 6.5% of revenue to protect the asset base, NWC held at 30.5% from the latest balance sheet rather than reverting down); bear and bull shock the same three drivers with the revenue asymmetry argued on the Tirta customer step-change [S3][S0].

findings.finding: The DCF discounting is mid-year, not full-year off the 2026-11-14 asof date: the FY2026E row carries a 0.2519 time fraction and the FY2027E row 0.9966. The DCF therefore starts almost a year after the pack date and the FY2026E cash flow is barely discounted.

The peer median P/E of 8.50x rests on 9 names with a 5.75x-23.08x spread, and only 10 of 19 MATERIALS_OTHER peers carry an EV/EBITDA at all (median 11.74x). The method weight is 5% so the impact is small, but the cross-check sample is thin.

The 2026Q2 anomaly (revenue 205.3bn, gross margin 29.7%, net profit 38.8bn, receivables +81bn, operating cash flow -10.1bn) is disclosed but has no sourced cause; the report treats it as a one-off on inference.

flags.message: a.cost_of_debt: bear 0.02 vs bull -0.005 is lopsided — mirror the shock or justify the asymmetry
flags.justification: The bear's +200bp is the renewal risk on the Bank Pan recurring facility, contracted at 7.25% to 11 March 2026 and secured on personal guarantees from the controlling shareholder, so repricing is one-sided in the evidence we can source; the bull's -50bp reflects the house macro deck's easing path for the policy rate rather than a lower spread, and is deliberately smaller than the bear [S3].

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'dcf_fcff': 0.6, 'ev_ebitda': 0.2, 'pe': 0.2}
flags.justification: The peer median P/E multiple of 8.5x yields a value 53% below the DCF because it capitalises trailing earnings from the expansion trough year and ignores the working-capital charge; we reduce its weight to a token 5% and raise the DCF weight to 75% because the DCF is the only method that captures the receivables build, which is the central cash-flow issue the 2026 quarterly accounts reveal [S0][S3].
